items.question: Was the research published in a credible venue?
items.rationale: The study is an IEEE conference paper with a DOI in the IEEE Aerospace Conference series.
evidence: Included corpus metadata reports DOI 10.1109/aero.2017.7943691.

items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The paper explicitly states assumptions about intended users, notes services outside the CRM scope, states that relationships are illustrative, and places substantial validation work in future work.
evidence: The model is being developed under the assumption that the members of the team have an intermediate-level understanding of space mission analysis and design, ModelBased Systems Engineering (MBSE), and Systems Modeling Language (SysML) and that they are working with subject matter experts who are guiding them through this effort.
There are other services that are not specific to a CubeSat project and are not explicitly modeled in the CRM, but if they are important to the mission, they can and should be modeled by the users.
These relationships between elements are illustrative not prescriptive.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The CubeSat form factor, target university/team context, mission enterprise, space/ground segments, and development flow from logical architecture to physical architecture and development are described.
evidence: A CubeSat, a type of nanosatellite, is a low-cost standardized satellite with its origin in the CubeSat Project which was established in 1999 by California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly), San Luis Obispo and Stanford University's Space and Systems Development Laboratory (SSDL).
The basic CubeSat unit is 10x10x10 centimeters with a mass of about 1.3 kilograms, and this cubic unit is referred to as 1U.
The CRM logical elements are a starting point for a mission-specific CubeSat logical architecture, followed by the physical architecture and the CubeSat development.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: SysML, No Magic tooling, package organization, diagram families, and mission-specific modeling steps are described, but the engineering methodology is not detailed, relationships are explicitly non-prescriptive, and complete model assets or implementation instructions are not provided.
evidence: SSWG's application of MBSE is enabled by the following: 1) a modeling language - SysML, 2) an engineering methodology, and 3) a modeling tool set from No Magic, Inc.

Figure 4 shows the CRM's high-level organization. There are packages for the Enterprise, Segments, and Subsystems. These packages contain packages for behaviors, structures validation, and verification.
These relationships between elements are illustrative not prescriptive.

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claims about reuse, reduced burden, consistency, objective V&V evidence, and scenario execution are tied to the CRM, SysML model elements, viewpoints, and model-enabled mission scenarios.
evidence: The CRM will have logical elements that can be reused by a mission-specific CubeSat team as a basis for its logical and physical CubeSat models.
Figure 10 illustrates that viewpoints into the CRM will provide the objective evidence needed for validation.

MBSE holds the promise of reducing the burden of systems engineering tasks, which is beneficial to small CubeSat teams, and a properly designed reference model can serve as a checklist to these teams and promote uniformity and consistency across future CubeSat models.

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper shows conceptual SysML artifacts and cites/prior work on simulation, but most evaluations are described in future tense; no metrics, baseline comparison, completed stakeholder evaluation, integration test, or flight data are reported for the current CRM.
evidence: Previously, the SSWG demonstrated the ability to model behaviors, interface with commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) simulation tools, and carry out trade studies [2].

CRM validation and verification of the CRM will include populating it with an example mission to evaluate the completeness of the CRM SysML elements and also providing it to several university team (currently four) for evaluation.
Arrangements are being made for the CRM to be evaluated by SysML and MBSE experts.

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: The paper centers the CRM on trace/refine/derive relationships among stakeholder needs, objectives, measures, requirements, use cases, segments, subsystems, validation, and verification viewpoints.
evidence: Mission use cases are created to refine mission requirements which support the measures of effectiveness, objectives, needs, and constraints.
Space and ground subsystem requirements are derived from segment requirements and trace to segment use cases.

The CRM will have viewpoints for model elements and relationships in support of mission-specific CubeSat stakeholder needs, objectives, and technical elements as well as requirements definition, validation, and verification.

items.question: Are model availability, open-source assets, reusable packages, data exchange mechanisms, or sufficient implementation details reported to assess reproducibility and toolchain continuity?
items.rationale: The study reports reusable CRM packages, a reference-information model, No Magic tooling, meeting materials, and planned OMG specification, but it does not provide a public model file, exchange format, versioned package, or complete reproduction procedure.
evidence: Meeting materials and links to meeting recordings are in Google Docs. Conference papers are posted on the INCOSE SSWG website.
Develop the CRM as an Object Management Group (OMG) specification.
A CubeSat Reference Information model, as shown in Figure 5, has been created to accompany the CRM.

quality_checklist.overall_rationale: The paper is a credible, scope-aware interim report with clear CubeSat context, SysML artifacts, traceability concepts, and reusable reference-model mechanisms. Its main weaknesses for evidence synthesis are the lack of completed outcome evaluation, limited reproducibility details, and only high-level toolchain/method implementation information.

bibliographic_review_management.status_rationale: Retained as core because it directly addresses CubeSat MBSE reference modeling, reuse, traceability, and model-integrated V&V at system level; EPS relevance is limited to a high-level Power Subsystem block and generic subsystem requirements.
bibliographic_review_management.citation: Kaslow, D., Hart, L., Ayres, B., Cahill, P. T., & Yntema, R. (2017). Developing a CubeSat Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) Reference Model - Interim Status #3. IEEE Aerospace Conference. https://doi.org/10.1109/aero.2017.7943691
bibliographic_review_management.title: Developing a CubeSat Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) Reference Model - Interim Status #3

RQ1.rationale: The paper gives a general CubeSat mission reference model and mission-specific instantiation pathway, but it is not EPS-specific and assumes intermediate space-mission, MBSE, and SysML knowledge with SME support.

RQ2.rationale: It claims reuse, uniformity, consistency, reduced systems-engineering burden, and tool/model integration at CubeSat system level, but not EPS reliability outcomes and without quantitative evidence.

RQ3.rationale: It describes model-integrated validation/verification via packages, viewpoints, traces, representative missions, and V&V scenarios before physical development, but not for EPS specifically.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: This is an interim-status paper in an SSWG CubeSat Reference Model series and explicitly builds on prior interim, behavior-modeling, and simulation/trade-study work cited in the references; no prior extraction or other papers were consulted.

space segment, CubeSat, spacecraft-bus subsystems, and ground segment subsystems

mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.system_boundary_level_of_abstraction: The CRM provides a logical architecture whose components are abstractions of physical components without implementation constraints; mission teams instantiate enterprise-to-subsystem logical elements and later define physical hardware, software, persistent data, and procedures.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.minimal_or_excluded_modeling: Other services not specific to a CubeSat project are not explicitly modeled unless important to a mission; subsystem definitions are broad; element relationships are illustrative rather than prescriptive; detailed physical components are deferred to mission-specific modeling.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.required_prior_behavioral_domain_knowled: Intermediate-level understanding of space mission analysis and design, MBSE, and SysML, plus guidance from subject matter experts.
mbse_objective_scope_artifacts.handling_limited_behavioral_knowledge: The paper handles behavioral modeling through a reusable reference logical architecture, requirements-to-use-case refinement, use case descriptions, scenario modeling, activity decomposition, and broad subsystem starting points that teams can modify; it does not provide a method requiring no behavioral/domain knowledge.

RQ1: A general CubeSat mission can be modeled by instantiating a reusable SysML CRM covering domain, enterprise, external constraints, space/ground segments, subsystems, requirements, measures, use cases, and logical-to-physical architecture transitions.

The Power Subsystem is included only as a high-level spacecraft-bus subsystem with the function to generate, regulate, store, and distribute power; no EPS architecture, behavior, power budget, or component model is provided.
The approach does not minimize required knowledge to novice level; it assumes intermediate space-mission, MBSE, and SysML understanding plus subject-matter expert guidance.
RQ2: Claimed MBSE outcomes include reusable starting points, consistency/uniformity across future models, reduced systems-engineering burden, model-centered requirements/design, and integration with external models/tools.
The paper does not provide EPS-specific reliability, reproducibility, or integrability outcomes and provides no quantitative outcome evidence or baseline comparison.
Reproducibility is planned through CRM reuse, reference information, and OMG specification ambitions, but actual public model assets and repeated-use evidence are not reported.
RQ3: Verification is integrated at the model level through validation/verification packages, requirements traceability, viewpoints, representative mission population, V&V scenarios, and possible executable mission modeling with COTS tools.
Verification methods are stated generically as inspection, analysis, demonstration, and test, and mission-specific teams are responsible for regulatory compliance verification.
No EPS-specific pre-physical verification procedures, power-subsystem test cases, or electrical integration checks are reported.
